extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of poetics, and critics of drama
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical guidance for composing tragedy: plot construction, recognition, diction, chorus, performance, and the use of stylistic devices. Focused on classical tragic drama but applicable as general principles for dramatic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality of stage actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing done upon the stage should appear to be without a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is absolutely necessary that something be shown for which there is no apparent cause, make it something that happened before the period of the play's commencement so it will not seem arbitrarily introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character idealization and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of better men; the poet should produce an example of moderation rather than extreme roughness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the peculiarity of character but bring forward the finest parts and keep the bad parts out of sight. Imitate portrayers who make their subjects appear handsomer than the originals by emphasizing appropriate traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) — types and preferability
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several sorts of recognition: by natural marks (scars, tokens), by poet-invented signs, by memory, by reasoning, and by the false calculation of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognition produced by the incidents and changes of situation (peripeteia) rather than marks or devices invented by the poet. Recognition should arise from the plot's events so it feels organic; poet-invented arbitrary tokens are less artistic and may cause error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot unity and connection of episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet ought to connect his story and see that episodes are suitable and in strict connection with the principal story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce episodes except those in strict relation to the main action; too many episodes destroy unity. Avoid making a tragedy into an epic by including many unrelated stories; select and limit incidents so the piece retains unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: plot and unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has two component parts: the plot (up to the change of fortune) and the unravelling (from that change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange the incidents so the plot leads to a clear change (peripeteia) and the unravelling follows naturally; identify the circumstances supposed to have occurred before the play and those within it that form the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal justification of incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: At the occurrence of every adventure the poet ought to ask himself why it was introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the poet cannot give a satisfactory answer for an incident's presence, he may be assured it has no business there. Imagine oneself a witness of the performance and remove anything that cannot be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for complex plots (peripeteia + recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of tragedy (complex, pathetic, moral, and others), and the complex—made up of peripeteia and recognition—is especially important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to master all kinds, but especially the principal forms; peripeteia and recognition compose the strongest complex tragedy, whereas simple plots lack changes in knowledge or circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as part of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus should be considered one of the actors and a part of the whole performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral songs must relate solely to what is going on and help elucidate the piece; they should be interested spectators that carry on the performance, not indifferent observers or unrelated song-insertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture and vivid representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should, as much as possible, make the player assist his speech with gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine scenes with minute attention and picture them as if present at their representation; actors who are themselves affected by passions will better move the audience. Weaknesses in staging (e.g., omitted circumstances) can condemn a piece at performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment and the excitation of passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters relating to sentiment (pity, fear, anger, making things great or small) should be produced by reasoning and the events of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same forms as the orator (demonstration, refutation, exciting the passions) but the occurrences must appear pitiable or terrible by themselves in the performance—rather than being proved so by speech alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence of discourse: perspicuity and nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of discourse is that it be perspicuous and not mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perspicuity comes from the use of proper, common words; nobility arises from uncommon expressions (foreign words, metaphor, ornament). Avoid extremes: all-metaphor yields a riddle, all-foreign yields barbarism. Maintain a medium and mix forms in moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery and proper use of metaphor and stylistic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: To have command of metaphor is a sign of ready genius; other forms (double words, foreign expressions, ornament, extended/contracted words) are tools to be used rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double words, foreign expressions, metaphor, ornament, and other devices should be employed properly and in moderation. Incorrect or excessive use produces ridicule or barbarism; correct use gives freedom from vulgarity and nobility to diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre- and meter-appropriate diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of diction suit different genres: double words for dithyrambics, foreign for heroic, metaphor for iambic poems; iambic imitates conversation and should use words suitable to speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose devices appropriate to the genre and meter: heroic may employ a wider variety, while iambic should principally use common expressions, metaphor, and ornament to imitate conversation naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the whole as a connected sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem (or dramatic work) ought to be a connected whole—a 'sentence'—that signifies a single object by connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the whole composition is unified so that its parts cohere into one single effect or object (the Iliad being an example of a connected whole by extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid audience false-calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on the audience's mistaken expectations to produce recognition or effect (the false messenger case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recognitions and revelations so they arise legitimately from events; don't contrive devices that depend on the audience making a wrong calculation about what will happen.
